description_full: Village Farms International, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, produces, markets, and distributes greenhouse grown tomatoes, bell peppers, and cucumbers in North America and Netherlands. It operates in five segments: Cannabis-Canada, Cannabis-U.S., Cannabis  Netherlands, Produce, and Clean Energy. It produces and supplies cannabis products to other licensed providers and provincial governments in Canada and internationally; develops and sells cannabinoid-based health and wellness products, including ingestible, edibles, and topical applications; and produces power. The company also markets and distributes its products under the Village Farms brand name to retail supermarkets and fresh food distribution companies. In addition, it produces and supplies cannabis products to designated coffee shops. Village Farms International, Inc. was founded in 1989 and is headquartered in Lake Mary, Florida.

financial_summary: Village Farms International, In is a small-cap consumer defensive business with a $352M market cap on $216M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -10% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are expanding by +3.3pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.

Returns on capital run at -7% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 12% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $40M in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.79× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 13× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.8%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 10% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
